newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan, Japan to discuss islands row in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan, Japan to discuss islands row in Tokyo.

text.p: Taiwan and Japan will hold talks in Tokyo on Friday to discuss issues arising from their rival claims to a chain of East China Sea islands, the Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday.
"According to information I received this morning, the Taiwan-Japan talks will definitely be held, and they will be held in Tokyo," Foreign Minister John Chang said on state television.
"Both sides want the talks to occur as soon as possible. We hope to have the talks tomorrow or the day after," he added.
Ministry spokesman Peter Cheng confirmed that Taipei and Tokyo had agreed to meet at 10 a.m. (0200 GMT) on Friday.
A seven-member negotiating team from the Foreign Ministry, Interior Ninistry and Council of Agriculture would leave for Tokyo on Thursday, Cheng said.

The meetings, expected to last for one or two days, would be the second round since the dispute flared in July over ownership of the uninhabited islands claimed by Japan as the Senkakus and by Taiwan and China as the Diaoyus.
Fishing rights, not rival claims to the islands themselves, are expected to top the agenda as Tokyo regards its claim of sovereignty to be closed to negotiation.
But the sovereignty dispute is sure to suffuse the talks.

Japanese rightists triggered an angry and increasingly nationalistic backlash from Chinese around Asia after raising Japan's flag and building a makeshift lighthouse on the islands in July to bolster Tokyo's claim.

Taiwan fishermen complain that Japanese patrol boats have barred them from fishing near the islands. The Japanese patrols also have repulsed boats trying to land Taiwan and Hong Kong protesters on the islands, deepening anti-Japanese resentment.
Taiwan activists have pledged to make another attempt to land on the islands on October 6.

Japan recognises only Beijing and has no diplomatic ties with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government. But they share close economic, social and cultural ties managed by representative offices that double as consular outposts.
The sovereignty row took on new urgency on September 26 when a Hong Kong activist, whose boat was turned away by Japanese patrol vessels, jumped into waters near the islands and drowned.
Japan took the islands as war booty after defeating imperial China in 1895 and refuses to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.
China and Taiwan, separated by a civil war in 1949, say the islands have been Chinese territory for centuries and should have been returned after Japan's World War Two defeat.
